title: IDS and IPS alerts
quick: An IDS watches network traffic and raises an alert when something matches a rule or looks unusual. An IPS sits in the path of traffic and can also block it. An alert is a lead to check, not proof.

sections.title: IDS and IPS
text: An intrusion detection system (IDS) detects and reports. An intrusion prevention system (IPS) works inline with traffic and can stop it as well (NIST SP 800-94). Suricata is one engine that can run in both ways and can also process saved PCAP files.
Systems can be network based or placed on a host.

sections.title: How alerts are made
text: Most alerts come from rules that describe a pattern in traffic. Some systems also look for unusual behaviour. When a rule matches, the system writes an alert with the time, addresses, ports and the rule name.
Good practice is to keep the matching packets or the rule details so the alert can be explained later.

sections.title: Reading an alert
text: Check these points before trusting an alert.
points: Which rule fired and what does it look for.
The time and the clock source.
Source and destination, and whether address translation hides the real host.
Whether traffic was blocked or only seen.
Other logs from the same time.

sections.title: False positives and negatives
text: A false positive is an alert for harmless traffic. A false negative is a missed attack. Both happen. Rules also age, so replaying a capture with new rules can give new results. Record the rule set version used.

compare.title: IDS and IPS
rows: A wrong block can stop normal traffic

mistakes: Treating an alert as proof of an attack.
Ignoring false positives and not checking the packets.
Not noting the rule set version or time source.
Forgetting that encrypted traffic limits what rules can see.

terms.meaning: A system that detects suspicious traffic and reports it.
A system that can also block suspicious traffic.
A rule that matches a known pattern.
An alert raised for harmless activity.
A device or program that watches traffic and sends alerts.

exam.q: What is the main difference between IDS and IPS?
exam.a: An IDS detects and alerts. An IPS is placed inline and can also block traffic.

exam.q: Why can you not rely on an alert alone?
exam.a: Rules can fire on harmless traffic, so the alert must be checked against packets and other logs.
